summary: Specifies Atom, an XML-based format for syndicating web content and metadata, such as news feeds and blog posts. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for websites to publish a list of new posts in a standard format, so a reader app can show you everything new without visiting each site.

questions: what is the atom syndication format
what is atom id used for
subtitle: An XML format for feeds of entries, so readers can follow new posts and news from many sites in one place.

tldr.problem: Weblogs and news sites want to publish lists of new items in a standard way, so that web sites and user agents can pick them up without scraping pages.
tldr.mechanism: Atom defines an XML format where a feed holds feed-level metadata and a series of entries. Each entry has required fields such as a unique id, a title and an updated time, plus optional content, authors, links and categories.
tldr.outcome: Atom documents use the application/atom+xml media type and can be extended with foreign markup, signed and encrypted. The RFC has been updated by RFC 5988.

today: RFC 4287 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5988. It remains the definition of the Atom Syndication Format as of that update.

sections.title: What Atom Describes
sections.content:
Atom is an XML-based document format that describes lists of related information called feeds. A feed is made of entries, each with an extensible set of metadata attached. For example, each entry has a title.

The primary use case is the syndication of web content such as weblogs and news headlines, both to web sites and directly to user agents. The format lives in the XML namespace http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom, and may be called "Atom 1.0" for convenience.

Conformance is defined for two artifacts, Atom Feed Documents and Atom Entry Documents, and the RFC also places requirements on Atom Processors. Fragments of a RELAX NG Compact schema illustrate the text, but the text itself defines conformance. The complete schema is in Appendix B.
sections.plainLanguage: A feed is like a newspaper's list of headlines, and each entry is one headline with its details. Atom is the agreed way to write that list so any app can read it.

sections.title: Atom Documents, IRIs and Base URIs
sections.content:
An Atom Feed Document represents a feed: metadata about it plus some or all of its entries, with atom:feed as the root. An Atom Entry Document represents exactly one entry outside any feed, with atom:entry as the root. Both are serialized as XML 1.0, identified with the application/atom+xml media type, and MUST be well-formed XML. No DTD is defined, so documents need not be valid in the XML sense.

Atom allows IRIs (RFC 3987); every URI (RFC 3986) is also an IRI. An IRI that is not a URI MUST be mapped to a URI before it is dereferenced, but an IRI used as an atom:id MUST NOT be mapped, so that comparison works. Any element MAY carry xml:base to set the base for relative references and xml:lang to give the natural language.

How processors combine several feed documents to rebuild a feed is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A feed document is the whole newspaper page, and an entry document is one clipped story. Both are written as tidy XML so computers can read them.

sections.title: Common Constructs: Text, People and Dates
sections.content:
Several elements share three building blocks. A Text construct holds human-readable text and has a type of text (the default), html or xhtml. Plain text must have no child elements; html content has no child elements either and its markup must be escaped; xhtml content must be a single XHTML div element, which is not itself part of the content. MIME media types MUST NOT be used as the type here.

A Person construct describes a person or similar entity. It MUST contain exactly one atom:name, and MAY contain one atom:uri and one atom:email.

A Date construct follows the date-time production of RFC 3339, with an uppercase T between date and time and an uppercase Z when there is no numeric offset, for example 2003-12-13T18:30:02Z. Dates SHOULD be as accurate as possible. There MUST NOT be any white space in a Date construct or any IRI.
sections.plainLanguage: Atom reuses three small forms: one for text, one for who someone is, and one for when something happened. Each has strict rules, so every app reads them the same way.

sections.title: Feeds, Entries and Content
sections.content:
An atom:feed contains metadata elements followed by zero or more atom:entry elements. It MUST contain exactly one atom:id, one atom:title and one atom:updated. It MUST contain one or more atom:author elements unless every entry has its own author. It SHOULD contain a link with rel="self", the preferred URI for retrieving the feed.

An atom:entry MUST contain exactly one atom:id, atom:title and atom:updated. An entry with no atom:content MUST have at least one rel="alternate" link. It MUST have an atom:summary when its content is out-of-line (it has a src attribute) or Base64-encoded. If several entries in a document share one atom:id, they represent the same entry, and a processor might show only the one with the latest atom:updated.

The atom:content element either holds the content or links to it with src. Its type can be text, html, xhtml, or a non-composite MIME media type; with no type or src it is treated as text. XML media types may contain child elements, text/ types must not, and all other types MUST be valid Base64.
sections.plainLanguage: A feed is a folder with a name, an ID and a last-changed time. Each entry inside is a note with its own name, ID and time, and either the text itself or a pointer to where it lives.

sections.title: Metadata Elements: IDs, Links and More
sections.content:
The atom:id is a permanent, universally unique identifier and MUST be an IRI. It MUST NOT change when a document is relocated, republished or imported. Processors MUST NOT assume it can be dereferenced, and MUST compare ids character by character, case-sensitively. So http://www.example.org/thing and http://www.example.org/Thing are different identifiers.

The atom:updated element records the most recent instant when the publisher modified the entry or feed in a way it considers significant. atom:published marks an event early in the entry's life, typically its creation or first availability.

The atom:link element requires an href. It MAY have rel (defaulting to alternate), type, hreflang, title and length. Other elements include atom:author and atom:contributor (Person constructs), atom:category (with a required term), atom:generator, atom:icon (aspect ratio of one to one), atom:logo (aspect ratio of two to one), atom:rights, atom:subtitle and atom:summary.

The atom:source element lets an entry copied from one feed into another keep information about its origin. Aggregators SHOULD include at least the source's atom:id, atom:title and atom:updated.
sections.plainLanguage: Each entry has a name tag that never changes, so apps can tell if they have seen it before. Links point to related pages, and other labels say who wrote it and when.

sections.title: Signing and Encrypting Atom Documents
sections.content:
Because Atom is XML, existing XML security mechanisms apply. The root of an Atom Document, or any atom:entry, MAY carry an enveloped XML digital signature. Processors MUST NOT reject a document just because they cannot verify such a signature. Those that do verify MUST support exclusive XML canonicalization and MUST be able to verify RSA signatures, though not necessarily DSA. Documents SHOULD NOT use MACs for signatures.

The root of an Atom Document MAY also be encrypted with XML Encryption. Processors that decrypt MUST be able to decrypt with AES-128 in CBC mode. Because such encryption does not ensure integrity, they SHOULD check a signature hash or a hash inside the document.

When a document is both signed and encrypted, it is generally a good idea to sign first and then encrypt. If MACs are used, that order is required.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature is a seal that shows who wrote a message and that it was not changed. Encryption is a lock so only the right reader can open it. Seal first, then lock.

sections.title: Extending Atom
sections.content:
Atom allows markup from other vocabularies, called foreign markup, anywhere except where it is explicitly forbidden. The Atom namespace itself is reserved for future forward-compatible revisions, and unrecognized Atom-namespace markup is treated as foreign markup.

Processors that meet foreign markup in a legal location MUST NOT stop or signal an error. If they cannot process it, they MAY bypass it when it appears as a child of an entry, feed or Person construct, and SHOULD ignore the markup but keep the text when it appears inside a Text construct or atom:content.

Extension elements come in two kinds. A Simple Extension has no attributes or child elements and acts like a name and value pair of its parent. A Structured Extension has at least one attribute or child element, and its meaning is defined by the extension's own specification.
sections.plainLanguage: You can add your own labels to an Atom feed. Apps that do not know them just skip them without breaking.

sections.title: Security and Media Type Registration
sections.content:
Text constructs and atom:content can deliver HTML and XHTML, and many elements in those languages are unsafe. The RFC says processors should pay particular attention to IMG, SCRIPT, EMBED, OBJECT, FRAME, FRAMESET, IFRAME, META and LINK, because (X)HTML can contain or reference executable content.

It also warns about spoofing: an attacker may publish an entry with the atom:id of an entry from another feed, perhaps with a falsified atom:source. A processor that hides duplicates by id should consider checking whether the entries came from the same publisher.

IANA registered the application/atom+xml media type with the file extension .atom, and created a Registry of Link Relations holding the five initial values alternate, related, self, enclosure and via.
sections.plainLanguage: A feed can carry web page code, and some of it is risky. Apps should be careful about what they run, and should not trust an entry only because it uses a familiar ID.

data.title: Atom Feed Document
data.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<feed xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom">

  <title>Example Feed</title>
  <link href="http://example.org/"/>
  <updated>2003-12-13T18:30:02Z</updated>
  <author>
    <name>John Doe</name>
  </author>
  <id>urn:uuid:60a76c80-d399-11d9-b93C-0003939e0af6</id>

  <entry>
    <title>Atom-Powered Robots Run Amok</title>
    <link href="http://example.org/2003/12/13/atom03"/>
    <id>urn:uuid:1225c695-cfb8-4ebb-aaaa-80da344efa6a</id>
    <updated>2003-12-13T18:30:02Z</updated>
    <summary>Some text.</summary>
  </entry>

</feed>

viz.caption: REQUIRED AND COMMON PARTS OF A FEED

root.label: atom:feed
root.note: root of an Atom Feed Document

children.label: atom:author
children.note: required unless every entry has one

items.label: Alternate
items.desc: An alternate version of the described resource. Default when rel is absent.

items.label: Related
items.desc: A resource related to the described resource.

items.label: Self
items.desc: A resource equivalent to the containing element.

items.label: Enclosure
items.desc: A related resource that may be large and need special handling; length SHOULD be given.

items.label: Via
items.desc: The source of the information in the containing element.
